title: Teach Us to Pray; Signs, Light, and Woes
summary: Jesus teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer in its shorter Lukan form and urges bold asking of a Father who gives the Holy Spirit. Accused of driving out demons by Beelzebul, he answers that he does so by the finger of God and that the kingdom has come upon his hearers. He warns a generation demanding signs that only the sign of Jonah will be given, speaks of the eye as the lamp of the body, and at a Pharisee's table pronounces woes on Pharisees and experts in the law.
story:
Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, teaching as he goes. Chapter 10 ended with Mary at his feet listening to his word; this chapter opens with Jesus himself at prayer and a disciple asking to be taught to pray. Luke shows Jesus praying at every turning point, at his baptism (3:21), before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), and at the transfiguration (9:28-29), and now the disciples ask to share it. Prayer fills the first thirteen verses.

The rest of the chapter turns to conflict, and it shows two responses to Jesus side by side: humble asking and suspicious testing. The charge that Jesus works by Satan's power and the demand for a sign from heaven show opposition hardening in the crowds, and a meal in a Pharisee's house ends in a sharp exchange that leaves the scribes and Pharisees lying in wait to catch him. The chapter's two halves are joined by the word ask: the disciples are told that everyone who asks receives, while this generation asks for a sign and will receive none but Jonah's. Chapter 12 follows directly, with a crowd of thousands and warnings about the leaven of the Pharisees.
historical:
Jewish prayer in Jesus' day was already rich and patterned. Devout Jews recited the Shema morning and evening and prayed the Tefillah, the Eighteen Benedictions later called the Amidah, at fixed times (m. Berakhot 4:1). Its sixth blessing asks the Father to forgive, for we have sinned, and its ninth asks for a year of good produce. The Kaddish, an Aramaic prayer attested later but probably old in its core, prays that God's great name be magnified and sanctified and that he establish his kingdom in your lifetime. Groups and teachers had their own prayers, as the disciples' reference to John's teaching shows, and the Qumran community left collections of hymns and liturgies. The prayer Jesus gives is short, addressed simply to Father, and its first two petitions echo the Kaddish, while its requests for bread, forgiveness, and protection echo the Tefillah. Jakob Petuchowski and Michael Brocke collected Jewish and Christian studies of these parallels in The Lord's Prayer and Jewish Liturgy (1978). The Didache, a church manual from around AD 100, gives Matthew's longer form with a closing praise to God's power and glory and tells Christians to pray it three times a day (Didache 8.2-3).

Matthew places the prayer in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:9-13) and Luke on the road in answer to a request. Some scholars think Jesus taught it on more than one occasion; others think one teaching was handed down in two church traditions, Luke's closer to the original length and Matthew's to its liturgical fullness. The form English-speaking churches pray follows Matthew, with the closing praise added from later manuscripts and early church use.

Beelzebul (verses 15, 18, 19) is the name the accusers give to the prince of demons. It is related to Baal-zebub, lord of flies, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron consulted by King Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:2-16). Ugaritic texts from the thirteenth century BC call Baal zbl, prince, so many scholars take Baal-zebub as a mocking alteration of Baal-zebul, Prince Baal, while zebul also means an exalted house (1 Kings 8:13), which suits Jesus' image of the strong man's house. Exorcism was practiced by other Jews, which gives force to Jesus' question about your sons (verse 19). Tobit 8:2-3 tells of a demon driven off by the smoke of a fish's heart and liver, Acts 19:13-16 of Jewish exorcists at Ephesus using the name of Jesus, and Josephus (Antiquities 8.45-49) of a Jew named Eleazar who drew a demon out through a man's nostrils with a ring and a root prescribed by Solomon, before Vespasian and his soldiers. The charge that Jesus' power came from an evil source outlived him: Justin Martyr says opponents called Jesus a magician (Dialogue with Trypho 69), and a baraita in the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a) remembers Yeshu as executed for sorcery and leading Israel astray.

In the woes, tithing of produce was commanded (Leviticus 27:30, Deuteronomy 14:22-23), and the Mishnah's general rule made liable whatever is food, is cultivated, and grows from the soil (m. Maaserot 1:1). Yet it lists rue among wild herbs exempt from tithes (m. Sheviit 9:1), so tithing it went beyond what the rules required. Graves conveyed impurity to anyone who touched or walked over them (Numbers 19:16), and the Mishnah says graves were marked with lime each spring before Passover so that pilgrims would not be defiled unaware (m. Shekalim 1:1, m. Maaser Sheni 5:1). Monuments to prophets and kings were being built in Jesus' time: Josephus tells how Herod, having tried to rob David's tomb, built a costly monument of white stone at its entrance (Antiquities 16.179-183), and the rock-cut monuments in the Kidron Valley date from this period. The Lives of the Prophets, probably from the first century, records where the prophets were thought to lie. Abel is the first murder in Scripture (Genesis 4:8-10), and Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20-22), is the last in Chronicles, which stands last in the traditional order of the Hebrew Bible (b. Bava Batra 14b); a later legend told that his blood seethed on the temple floor until the Babylonian conquest (b. Gittin 57b).
cultural:
The parable of the friend at midnight depends on village life. People traveled at night to avoid the heat, so a late arrival was ordinary. Bread was baked early for the day, often in a shared oven, and three small loaves made a meal for one guest. Hospitality to a guest was a matter of the whole village's honor, so the host who has nothing to set before his friend is in real trouble. A peasant family commonly slept together on a raised platform in a single room, with the door barred by a wooden or iron bolt; getting up to draw it would wake the household. The key word in verse 8, anaideia, means shamelessness, not persistence. Kenneth Bailey (Poet and Peasant, 1976) argued that it refers to the sleeper, who gets up to avoid the shame of refusing hospitality, while Klyne Snodgrass (Stories with Intent, 2008) and others hold that it describes the asker's shameless boldness. Either way, the parable argues from lesser to greater: if a reluctant neighbor gives, how much more will the Father.

The comparisons in verses 11 and 12 pair things that look alike: a fish and a snake, and an egg and a scorpion, whose body curls into a pale oval. Matthew's parallel has bread and a stone (Matthew 7:9). The woman who calls out in verse 27 uses a common way of honoring a man by blessing his mother; the Mishnah records Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai praising a disciple with the words happy is she who bore him (m. Avot 2:8).

The lamp of verse 33 was a small clay oil lamp, set on a stand to light a one-room house; the cellar or storage pit and the basket (modios, a grain measure of about nine liters) would hide it. Ancient writers from Plato onward often described the eye as sending out light, and the Bible speaks of a good eye as generous and an evil eye as grudging (Deuteronomy 15:9, Proverbs 22:9, where the Hebrew for generous is literally good of eye). The word Jesus uses for the healthy eye, haplous, belongs to a family of words for singleness and generosity.

The meal in verse 37 is the ariston, the late-morning or midday meal. The Pharisee is surprised that Jesus did not first wash; the verb is baptizō, to immerse or wash. Ritual hand-washing before ordinary meals was a Pharisaic practice (Mark 7:3-4), not a command of the Law for lay Israelites, and Jacob Neusner (From Politics to Piety, 1973) argued that the Pharisees of this period were marked above all by extending priestly purity to the everyday table. The chief seats in the synagogue were the front benches facing the congregation, and greetings in the marketplace carried titles of honor. The experts in the law (nomikoi) were the scribes who interpreted and applied the Torah, whose rulings could lighten or add to the practical burden of obedience.
literary:
The chapter has three main sections. The teaching on prayer (1-13) moves from a model prayer (1-4) to a parable (5-8), to sayings with three pairs of verbs, ask, seek, knock (9-10), and to a comparison from the lesser to the greater (11-13); the word Father frames the section at its start and end. Luke ends with the Father giving the Holy Spirit to those who ask, where Matthew 7:11 has good things, in keeping with Luke's emphasis on the Spirit, whom Jesus received at his baptism while praying (3:21-22) and whom the church will receive at Pentecost while praying (Acts 1:14, 2:1-4).

The controversy section (14-36) is built from sayings joined by theme and catchword: a divided kingdom, the finger of God, the stronger man, the gathering and scattering, the returning spirit, true blessedness, the sign of Jonah, and the lamp. Two responses to the exorcism are named in verses 15 and 16, the accusation and the demand for a sign, and Jesus answers the first in verses 17 to 26 and the second in verses 29 to 32. Between them the woman's blessing (27-28) restates the point of 8:21: blessedness belongs to those who hear the word of God and keep it, which is what Mary did in 10:39. Twice Jesus says that something greater is here, first than Solomon and then than Jonah. Luke keeps the historical order, the queen of the South before the men of Nineveh, where Matthew 12:41-42 puts Nineveh first, so that Luke's sequence ends on repentance.

The meal (37-54) is a symposium scene, a common setting in Greek literature for teaching at table that Luke uses often (7:36-50, 14:1-24). It holds six woes in two sets of three, first against Pharisees (42-44) and then against experts in the law (46-52), a form that recalls the woes of the prophets (Isaiah 5:8-23, Amos 6:1). Much of this material has parallels scattered through Matthew 6, 7, 12, and 23, and Luke's order differs throughout. The closing verses use the language of hunting: the scribes and Pharisees lie in wait to catch something from his mouth, preparing for the trap questions of chapter 20.

outline.t: The friend at midnight; ask, seek, knock
The returning spirit and true blessedness
Woes to the experts in the law

doctrines.note: Jesus teaches disciples to call God Father, to put his name and kingdom first, and then to ask for bread, forgiveness, and protection. Prayer is bold because the one who hears is a good Father (verses 9-13), and the prayer binds the one who prays to forgive others, since receiving mercy and showing it cannot be separated (verse 4).

The prayer asks for the kingdom to come (verse 2), and verse 20 announces that in Jesus' exorcisms it has already come upon his hearers. The kingdom is both a present reality breaking into the world and a future fullness still prayed for, and it advances as the stronger one overpowers the strong man and frees his captives.

The best gift the Father gives to those who ask is the Holy Spirit (verse 13), and Matthew's parallel to verse 20 names the Spirit of God where Luke has the finger of God (Matthew 12:28). The Spirit is God's own presence and power, promised to disciples who ask, and the gift that the church receives in Acts.

Jesus insists that the God who made the outside made the inside as well (verse 40). Holiness is not external cleanliness while the heart is full of greed, but justice and the love of God, without neglecting lesser duties (verse 42). He does not despise careful obedience; he refuses to let it replace mercy.

The Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation, because they responded to lesser light (verses 31-32). Privilege increases accountability, and the blood of the prophets will be required of the generation that rejects the one greater than the prophets (verses 50-51).

words.note: Patēr, father. It occurs about 414 times in the New Testament, 56 of them in Luke. Luke's prayer begins with the single vocative Father, without Matthew's our and in heaven, which many scholars think reflects the Aramaic abba that Jesus used in prayer (Mark 14:36) and that Paul says the Spirit teaches believers to cry (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6). Joachim Jeremias argued that abba was a child's intimate word; James Barr (1988) showed it was the ordinary adult word for father, intimate and respectful at once. Every prayer of Jesus whose words Luke records addresses God as Father (10:21, 22:42, 23:46, and in many manuscripts 23:34).

Epiousios, usually translated daily. It occurs only in the two forms of the Lord's Prayer (here and Matthew 6:11), and Origen (On Prayer 27) said it was found in no other Greek writer and seemed to have been coined by the evangelists. Bruce Metzger (1957) showed that the one claimed occurrence in a papyrus cannot be confirmed. Proposed senses are bread for the coming day, bread needed for existence, and bread for today. Jerome reported that the Gospel of the Hebrews had mahar, tomorrow, and his Vulgate rendered it supersubstantialem in Matthew but cotidianum in Luke. Luke's present imperative with day by day stresses repeated, ongoing dependence.

Opheilō, to owe, be indebted, be obligated. It occurs about 35 times in the New Testament. Matthew's prayer speaks of debts on both sides; Luke asks forgiveness for sins (hamartias) but promises to forgive everyone who is indebted to us. The Aramaic word for debt was also used for sin, and Luke keeps both, so that sin is seen as a debt owed to God and wrongs done to us as debts we release. Luke uses the same picture in the parable of the two debtors (7:41-43).

Peirasmos, testing, trial, temptation. It occurs 21 times in the New Testament, six in Luke. The same word covers the testing of faith by hardship and the enticement to sin, and English versions choose between them. In Luke the devil ends his testing of Jesus (4:13), seed on rocky ground falls away in a time of testing (8:13), and in Gethsemane Jesus twice tells the disciples to pray that they may not enter into temptation (22:40, 46). James 1:13 says God tempts no one, and the petition asks God not to bring his children into a trial that would overwhelm them.

Anaideia, shamelessness, impudence. This is its only New Testament use. In ordinary Greek it is always a fault, the lack of a proper sense of shame, and translations that render it persistence soften a bolder word. Whether it describes the asker who wakes a neighbor at midnight or the sleeper who will not bear the shame of refusing, the parable does not picture God as reluctant; it argues from a grudging neighbor to a generous Father.

Daktulos, finger. It occurs eight times in the New Testament. The finger of God is an Exodus phrase: Pharaoh's magicians admit it in the plague of gnats (Exodus 8:19), and God writes the tablets of the covenant with it (Exodus 31:18, Deuteronomy 9:10). Jesus' exorcisms are God's own hand at work, a new exodus of captives. Luke uses the word again in verse 46: the experts in the law will not lift a finger to lighten others' burdens, while God's finger sets people free.

Sēmeion, sign. It occurs about 77 times in the New Testament, eleven in Luke. The shepherds receive a sign (2:12), and Simeon calls the child a sign to be spoken against (2:34). Here others test Jesus by demanding a sign from heaven (verse 16), a proof on their terms, and Herod will later hope to see one (23:8). Jesus offers only the sign of Jonah, himself as the prophet whose presence and preaching call for repentance.

Haplous, single, simple, sound. It occurs only here and in Matthew 6:22. Its opposite in verse 34 is ponēros, evil or bad, and the pairing recalls the Jewish idiom of the good eye for generosity and the evil eye for stinginess. The related noun haplotēs means sincerity and generosity (Romans 12:8, 2 Corinthians 9:11). A healthy eye is both clear and undivided, and in context that means receptive to the light Jesus brings.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the Son who prays and who teaches others to call God Father as he does. The prayer he gives is not about himself, yet it is his own relation to the Father opened to his disciples, the fruit of 10:22, where the Son reveals the Father to whom he chooses. The promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask points ahead to Pentecost, where the risen Jesus pours out the Spirit he received from the Father (Acts 2:33).

In the Beelzebul controversy Jesus is the stronger one. John the Baptist had announced that one stronger than he was coming (3:16), and here Jesus uses the same comparative for the one who overpowers the strong man, strips him of the armor he trusted, and divides the plunder. The image draws on Isaiah 49:24-25, where the Lord himself takes the captives from the mighty. He acts by the finger of God, the power that humbled Pharaoh's magicians and wrote the covenant, so his exorcisms are a new exodus.

Twice he says that something greater is here. Solomon, the son of David, was remembered for wisdom and, in Jewish tradition known to Josephus, for power over demons; the Queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth to hear him (1 Kings 10:1-13). Jonah was the prophet at whose preaching a Gentile city repented (Jonah 3:5). Jesus claims to surpass both, the royal son of David and the prophet, and Matthew makes explicit that Jonah's three days in the fish point to his resurrection (Matthew 12:40), a connection the early church painted again and again on the walls of the Roman catacombs. In verse 49 Jesus speaks for the wisdom of God, and his words about the blood of the prophets from Abel to Zechariah foreshadow his own death at the hands of the leaders he addresses. The one who warns them is the last and greatest of the messengers, and his blood, as Hebrews 12:24 puts it, speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
interpretation:
The Lord's Prayer has been expounded more than any other passage of Scripture. Tertullian's On Prayer (around 200) called it a summary of the whole gospel, and Cyprian's On the Lord's Prayer (around 252) taught it as the church's common prayer. Origen's On Prayer (around 233) compared Luke's shorter form with Matthew's and treated epiousios as a word the evangelists coined. Gregory of Nyssa's sermons on the prayer knew a Lukan text asking that the Holy Spirit come and cleanse us. Augustine (Enchiridion 116) explained that Luke's five petitions contain Matthew's seven, since thy will be done restates the first two and deliver us from evil completes lead us not into temptation, and his Letter 130 to the widow Proba taught that the prayer shapes what we should desire. Jerome reported that the Gospel of the Hebrews read bread for tomorrow. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q.83 a.9) ordered the seven petitions as the pattern of all desire. The prayer became the heart of catechesis: Luther's Small Catechism (1529), Calvin's Institutes (3.20), the Heidelberg Catechism (1563), and the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647) all end with it. Gregory the Great set it in the Roman Mass immediately after the eucharistic prayer. Joachim Jeremias (The Prayers of Jesus, 1967) made abba central to Jesus' teaching, and James Barr (1988) corrected the idea that it meant daddy. In 2017 and 2019 the French and Italian Catholic bishops, with Pope Francis's approval, changed the petition about temptation to let us not enter into temptation and do not abandon us to temptation, reviving an old debate about the verb. Jewish scholars such as Jakob Petuchowski have noted how fully the prayer belongs to Jewish liturgy, and Igor Stravinsky set the Slavonic Pater Noster (1926).

The Beelzebul controversy gave Christian demonology its prince of devils; Milton's Paradise Lost (1667) makes Beelzebub Satan's chief lieutenant, and William Golding's Lord of the Flies (1954) takes its title from a rendering of the name. Jonah became one of the most common Old Testament figures in early Christian catacomb art, read as a picture of resurrection.

The woes have a darker history. Read as a portrait of Judaism, they fed what Jules Isaac (Jésus et Israël, 1948) called the teaching of contempt, and after the Holocaust the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) and many Protestant statements rejected that reading. Historians such as Jacob Neusner and E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977), and Amy-Jill Levine (The Misunderstood Jew, 2006; with Joseph Sievers, The Pharisees, 2021), have reconstructed the Pharisees as a lay renewal movement whose heirs shaped rabbinic Judaism, and have pressed Christians to hear the woes as prophetic warning within Israel that applies to the church as well. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1 to 13 in Year C (Proper 12).
text:
English Bibles differ most in the Lord's Prayer. The earliest witnesses to Luke, led by P75 and Codex Vaticanus, with the Latin Vulgate, and the form Origen discussed, have the short prayer printed in the BSB and most modern versions: Father, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, daily bread, forgiveness, and lead us not into temptation. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, fill it out from Matthew with ‘Our’, ‘which art in heaven’, ‘Thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth’, and ‘but deliver us from evil’; Codex Sinaiticus and some other early witnesses agree with the longer text at some of these points and not others. Because Christians prayed Matthew's form daily, copyists naturally conformed Luke to it, which is why the short form is judged original. No manuscript of Luke has the closing doxology. Two late minuscules (162 and 700) read in place of your kingdom come ‘may your Holy Spirit come upon us and cleanse us’, a reading Gregory of Nyssa and Maximus the Confessor knew, and Tertullian's discussion (Against Marcion 4.26) suggests that Marcion's Gospel had a petition for the Spirit. Most scholars think it came from a baptismal use of the prayer.

Elsewhere, in verse 11 the King James Version adds ‘If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone?’, borrowed from Matthew 7:9 and absent from P45, P75, and Codex Vaticanus. In verse 13 P45 and Codex Bezae read ‘a good gift’ and the Vulgate ‘a good spirit’ instead of the Holy Spirit. In verse 33 the words ‘or under a basket’ are missing from P45, P75, and some other witnesses and are omitted by the Tyndale House edition, though Sinaiticus and Vaticanus have them. The name in verses 15 to 19 is spelled Beelzeboul in most Greek manuscripts and Beezeboul in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; the Latin and Syriac versions assimilated it to the Baal-zebub of 2 Kings 1, which is why the KJV reads Beelzebub.

teach.big: Disciples pray to a good Father who gives his Spirit and whose kingdom has broken into the world in Jesus, while those who demand proof and guard their religion's outside miss the one greater than Solomon and Jonah who stands before them.

outline.t: Jesus teaches us to pray by giving us his own address to God, Father, and puts God's name and kingdom before our bread, our forgiveness, and our safety.
Prayer is bold because God is not a reluctant neighbor but a good Father, and the best gift he gives is himself in the Holy Spirit.
Jesus' power over evil is God's own hand freeing captives, and there is no neutral ground: whoever does not gather with him scatters.
An emptied life is not a safe life; blessing belongs to those who hear God's word and keep it.
Demanding signs is a way of refusing the sign already given; Gentiles who heeded lesser messengers will judge those who ignore the greater.
The light of Christ is not hidden, but only an undivided, generous eye receives it.
God made the inside as well as the outside, so careful religion without justice and love for God is a clean cup full of greed.
Those who interpret God's word for others are judged by whether they lift burdens, honor the prophets by heeding them, and open the door to knowledge rather than blocking it.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The Lord's Prayer is sometimes treated as a formula to be recited without thought and sometimes, in reaction, as a mere outline never to be prayed as written; Luke's introduction, when you pray, say, supports praying the words themselves and learning from their order. The parable of the friend at midnight is often preached as if God must be nagged into giving; its logic runs the other way, from a grudging neighbor to a generous Father. Ask, seek, knock is misused as a promise that God will grant whatever we name, which ignores verse 13, where the gift in view is the Holy Spirit, and ignores Jesus' own prayer in Gethsemane (22:42).

The Beelzebul passage has been used to label opponents as demonic, the very move Jesus' accusers made, and verses 24 to 26 are sometimes turned into detailed teaching about demons returning, when the point is that moral clean-up without receiving the stronger one leaves a person exposed. The woes are the gravest risk. Preached as a portrait of Jews or Judaism, they repeat the teaching of contempt; preached as a license for Christians to denounce others, they become the thing they condemn. They should be heard first by teachers and religious leaders in the church, since Jesus addresses the most earnest believers of his day.
teach.pastoral: Calling God Father will press on those whose fathers were absent, cruel, or abusive. Acknowledge that the word can hurt, and note that Jesus defines it by what the Father does: gives good gifts, forgives, feeds, protects, and never hands a child a snake. Some listeners will carry prayers that were not answered as they asked, including for healing that did not come; the text does not promise every request and should not be used to blame them for lack of faith. People troubled by fear of demons or by scrupulous anxiety about uncleanness need to hear that the stronger one has already bound the strong man, and that Jesus' concern is the heart's mercy, not ritual perfection.

hard.q: Are Jesus' woes fair to the Pharisees, and have they been used against Jewish people?
hard.a:
The objection is strong and comes from Jewish and Christian historians alike. The Pharisees were a respected lay movement devoted to living the Torah in daily life; their successors produced the Mishnah and shaped rabbinic Judaism. Jules Isaac (Jésus et Israël, 1948) showed how Christian preaching turned Gospel polemic into a teaching of contempt for Jews, and scholars such as E. P. Sanders (1977), Jacob Neusner, and Amy-Jill Levine (The Misunderstood Jew, 2006) have argued that the Gospels' picture of Pharisees as legalists and hypocrites is a caricature shaped by later conflict between church and synagogue. Christians used passages like this one for centuries to justify contempt, exclusion, and violence against Jewish communities.

Responses begin by reading Luke closely. Luke's Pharisees are not uniformly hostile: they invite Jesus to meals (7:36, 11:37, 14:1), warn him of Herod's plot (13:31), and in Acts include Gamaliel, who counsels restraint (Acts 5:34-39), believers (Acts 15:5), and Paul, who still calls himself a Pharisee (Acts 23:6). The woes are prophetic speech in Israel's own tradition, like Isaiah's and Amos's, spoken by a Jew to fellow Jews and aimed at particular failures: outward religion without mercy, burdens laid on others, and resistance to God's messengers. Jewish sources themselves criticize hypocritical piety; the Talmud lists seven kinds of Pharisees, most of them unflattering (b. Sotah 22b), and the Dead Sea Scrolls attack teachers they call seekers of smooth things. Most Christian traditions today, following Nostra Aetate (1965), reject any reading that makes these words a verdict on the Jewish people. Read in context, the woes call religious teachers of every age, the church's first of all, to justice and the love of God.

hard.q: Jesus says that everyone who asks receives. What about prayers that are not answered?
hard.a:
The skeptical case is simple and personal. Verses 9 and 10 promise without qualification that everyone who asks receives, yet believers pray for healing, rescue, and daily bread and do not receive them. Skeptics point to the Study of the Therapeutic Effects of Intercessory Prayer, a large trial led by Herbert Benson and published in the American Heart Journal in 2006, which found no difference in recovery between heart-surgery patients who were prayed for and those who were not; Richard Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006) presented it as evidence that petitionary prayer does nothing. On this view the promise is either false or so hedged by later qualifications that it means nothing.

Christian responses begin with the passage itself. Luke ends not with whatever you ask but with the Father giving the Holy Spirit to those who ask (verse 13), so the promise is first about God's gift of himself. The comparison is with a father, who gives what is good and refuses what would harm, and Jesus' own prayer in Gethsemane that the cup be removed was not granted as asked; he prayed it and then submitted to the Father's will (22:42). Augustine (Letter 130 to Proba) taught that prayer trains our desire to want what God gives. Theologians also note that a controlled trial treats prayer as a technique for testing God, which Jesus refused (4:12). Some Christian writers admit that the problem is not fully solved: C. S. Lewis, in Petitionary Prayer: A Problem Without an Answer (published in Christian Reflections, 1967), confessed that he could not reconcile the promises of confident asking with the pattern of thy will be done. The church has held both, praying boldly and submitting to the Father's will, as Jesus did.

observe: What does the disciple ask Jesus in verse 1, and what are the petitions of the prayer Jesus gives in reply?
What two responses to the exorcism do verses 15 and 16 record, and how does Jesus answer each?
What does Jesus say the Pharisees and the experts in the law do, and what does he say they neglect?
interpret: Why does the prayer put God's name and kingdom before our bread and forgiveness, and why does it tie our forgiveness to our forgiving others?
What does Jesus mean by the finger of God, and why does he say that whoever is not with him is against him?
In what sense is something greater than Solomon and Jonah present, and why will Gentiles judge this generation?
apply: Pray the Lord's Prayer slowly. Which petition is hardest for you to mean, and why?
Where have you asked God for signs on your own terms instead of responding to what he has already shown you?
Which of Jesus' woes, spoken to your church or to you, would land hardest, and what would repentance look like?
